title: Debugging & Bug Hunt: Map Pitfalls
summary: Troubleshoot HashMap memory leaks from missing hashCode/equals, mutable keys mutating in-place, and ConcurrentModificationException during iteration.
prerequisites: The Map Contract: Associative Key-Value Storage
The equals() and hashCode() Contract in Sets
learningObjectives: Identify and fix the 4 classic Map architecture bugs in production systems
Remediate memory leaks caused by mutating keys after HashMap insertion
Disambiguate missing keys from keys mapped to null values using containsKey()
expectedOutcomes: Intuitive ability to audit and remediate subtle Map identity and concurrency defects in enterprise codebases
Mastery of safe iteration and immutable key patterns in Java

activities.title: Practical Context: Post Office Box Rekeying Without Updating Directory

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Post Office Box Rekeying Without Updating Directory
analogy.story:
Imagine a post office with 1,000 locked PO Boxes. A customer rents Box #50, and their key code is registered in the master directory index.

One day, the customer secretly changes the physical lock on Box #50 to a different key code without notifying the post office. When the mail carrier sorts incoming letters, they look up the new key code in the directory, calculate that it belongs to Box #900, and drop the mail there. The customer visits Box #50, finds no mail, and reports the letters permanently lost.

This is identical to modifying a field in an object used as a HashMap key after it has already been inserted into the map.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Mutating fields used in a key's hashCode() changes its bucket address, stranding entries in orphaned buckets and causing permanent memory leaks.

activities.title: Map Bug Hunt: The 4 Classic Production Traps & Remediation

keyTakeaways: Trap 1: Mutating Map keys after insertion strands entries in wrong buckets and causes severe memory leaks
Trap 2: Calling map.remove(k) during for-each iteration throws ConcurrentModificationException
Trap 3: get(k) == null is ambiguous when null values are allowed; always check containsKey(k)
Trap 4: Inserting null keys or un-comparable keys into TreeMap causes NullPointerException or ClassCastException

activities.title: Remediating a Production In-Memory Cache Leak
activities.description: Trace an audit fixing a memory leak caused by mutable Map keys and improper iteration removal.

steps.description: Define an immutable record TenantKey to guarantee that hashCode() is permanent and immune to mutation.
Use explicit Iterator.remove() to evict expired items without triggering ConcurrentModificationException.
Verify expired tenant T1 is safely cleaned up, leaving only active tenant T2.

questions.question: What exception is thrown if you call map.remove(key) inside a standard for-each loop iterating over map.keySet()?
questions.explanation: Iterators maintain an expectedModCount. Calling map.remove() directly modifies modCount without updating expectedModCount, triggering ConcurrentModificationException on the next iteration.

questions.question: How do you distinguish between a key that is missing from a HashMap versus a key that maps to null?
options: They cannot be distinguished in Java
questions.explanation: map.containsKey(key) returns true if the key exists (even if its value is null), and false if the key was never inserted.

questions.question: Why does mutating a key object in a HashMap result in a memory leak?
options: Because the JVM disables garbage collection for all maps
Because the key's altered hash code points to the wrong bucket during map.remove(key), making it impossible to remove via normal methods while the map retains a strong reference
Because HashMap copies objects to disk
questions.explanation: remove(k) searches the bucket corresponding to the mutated hash code. Finding nothing, it does not remove the item from its original bucket, causing an unremovable memory leak.

questions.question: What is the recommended modern way to remove entries matching a condition from a Map in Java 8+?
options: Use reflection to set entries to null
questions.explanation: entrySet().removeIf(...) is concise, highly optimized, and safely manages internal iterator modification counts.

questions.question: How does ConcurrentModificationException occur in a single-threaded application?
questions.answer: ConcurrentModificationException has an unfortunate name: it does NOT require multiple threads! In a single thread, it occurs whenever a collection is structurally modified (adding or removing elements) through direct collection methods while an Iterator (like a for-each loop) is actively traversing it. The iterator detects that `modCount != expectedModCount` on `it.next()` and immediately fails fast to prevent reading corrupt state.

questions.question: Can you use an array (like byte[] or int[]) as a key in a HashMap? Why or why not?
questions.answer: Technically Java permits it, but practically it is a severe bug. Java arrays do not override equals() or hashCode()—they inherit the default implementation from Object, which checks reference identity (memory address). Two distinct arrays containing the exact same bytes will have different hash codes and return false on equals(). Therefore, `map.get(new byte[]{1, 2})` will never find an entry added with `map.put(new byte[]{1, 2}, val)`. To use byte sequences as keys, wrap them in java.nio.ByteBuffer or an immutable wrapper class.

questions.question: Why is String the most popular key type for HashMaps in Java?
questions.answer: String has three ideal properties for HashMap keys: 1) It is strictly immutable (its fields cannot change, preventing hash drift and vanishing entries), 2) Its hashCode() is cached in a private field `hash` after first computation, making subsequent lookups extremely fast, and 3) Its equals() and hashCode() are well-distributed and battle-tested.

I know how to safely remove entries during iteration using removeIf() or Iterator.remove()

practiceProblems.title: Safe In-Place Map Removal
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Fix the removeFailingGrades(Map<String, Integer> gradeMap, int threshold) method so it removes all students with grade < threshold without throwing ConcurrentModificationException.

practiceProblems.title: Accurate Null-Value Detection

hints: Do not use config.get(key) != null because the value itself may be null.

practiceProblems.title: Remediate Mutable Key Design

practiceProblems.title: Sanitize Keys for TreeMap Ingestion

hints: Check key == null before calling map.put().

practiceProblems.title: Diagnose Leaked Map Entries
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a map containing an entry whose key was mutated after insertion, implement findLeakedValueByLinearScan(Map<Key, Value> map, String targetKeyName) that locates the value by scanning entrySet() linearly.
